cards.q: Which parts of the eye refract light, and what kind of image forms on the retina?
cards.a: The cornea does most of the refracting; the lens makes the fine adjustment for focusing. The image on the retina is real, inverted and diminished.

cards.q: Compare rods and cones in the retina.
cards.a: Rods work in dim light, do not detect colour, and lie mostly away from the centre of the retina. Cones need brighter light, detect colour (three types), and are packed closely at the fovea.

cards.q: Explain why the eye resolves fine detail best at the fovea.
cards.a: The fovea has closely packed cones, each with its own nerve fibre.
marks: Two points are seen as separate only if their images fall on two receptors with at least one unstimulated receptor between them.
At the fovea the cones are very closely packed, so this happens for very small separations.
Each cone there connects to its own nerve fibre, so its signal reaches the brain separately.
Away from the fovea several rods share one nerve fibre, so their signals merge and detail is lost.

cards.q: What is myopia, and what kind of lens corrects it?
cards.a: Short sight: distant objects are focused in front of the retina, so they look blurred. It is corrected with a diverging lens.

cards.q: What is hypermetropia, and what kind of lens corrects it?
cards.a: Long sight: near objects would be focused behind the retina, so they look blurred. It is corrected with a converging lens.

cards.q: What is astigmatism, and how is it corrected?
cards.a: The cornea is curved by different amounts in different planes, so lines in one direction are in focus while lines in another are blurred. It is corrected with a cylindrical lens.
cards.why: A prescription for astigmatism gives the sphere power, the cylinder power and the angle of the cylinder's axis.

cards.q: Describe how sound is transmitted from the air to the auditory nerve.
cards.a: Through the ear canal, the eardrum, the ossicles and the fluid of the cochlea.
marks: The outer ear funnels sound waves down the ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates.
The three small bones of the middle ear (the ossicles) pass the vibrations to the oval window.
The oval window sets up pressure waves in the fluid of the cochlea.
These make hair cells on the basilar membrane move, producing electrical signals in the auditory nerve.

cards.q: How do the middle ear's ossicles increase the pressure of the sound reaching the inner ear?
cards.a: They act as a lever, increasing the force, and they pass it from the large eardrum to the much smaller oval window. A larger force on a smaller area gives a much greater pressure.

cards.q: The intensity of a sound doubles. By how much does its intensity level rise?
cards.a: By about 3 dB.
cards.why: 10log⁡2=3.0\displaystyle 10\log 2 = 3.010log2=3.0. Each tenfold increase in intensity adds 10 dB.

cards.q: Why is a logarithmic scale used for sound intensity level?
cards.a: The ear responds to ratios of intensity: each tenfold increase in intensity is heard as about the same step up in loudness. A logarithmic scale matches this, and it handles the enormous range of intensities the ear can detect.

cards.q: What is the dBA scale?
cards.a: A decibel scale adjusted to match the frequency response of the human ear, giving less weight to the frequencies the ear hears poorly.

cards.q: What does an equal loudness curve show, and what does its shape tell us about the ear?
cards.a: It shows the intensity level needed at each frequency for a sound to seem as loud as a reference tone at 1 kHz. The curve dips to a minimum at about 3 kHz, where the ear is most sensitive, and rises at low and high frequencies.

cards.q: How does hearing loss with age differ from hearing loss caused by exposure to excessive noise?
cards.a: With age, hearing is lost mainly at the higher frequencies. Noise damage causes a loss concentrated around 4 kHz (or the frequency of the noise). In both, the equal loudness curves are raised at the frequencies affected.

cards.q: State three things needed to obtain a good ECG trace.
cards.a: Good electrical contact with the skin (cleaned skin and conducting gel), a high-gain amplifier with a high input impedance because the signals are tiny, and a relaxed, still patient so other muscles do not add signals.

cards.q: Name the three parts of a normal ECG waveform and state what each corresponds to.
cards.a: P wave: the atria contract (depolarise). QRS wave: the ventricles contract (depolarise). T wave: the ventricles relax (repolarise).

cards.q: Explain why a gel is put between an ultrasound probe and the skin.
cards.a: Without it, almost all the ultrasound would be reflected at the skin.
marks: Air has a very different acoustic impedance from skin.
With an air gap, nearly all the ultrasound would be reflected and very little would enter the body.
The gel has an acoustic impedance close to that of skin and removes the air, so most of the ultrasound is transmitted.

cards.q: How does a piezoelectric crystal produce and detect ultrasound?
cards.a: Producing: an alternating potential difference across the crystal makes it change shape and vibrate, sending out ultrasound. Detecting: returning ultrasound makes the crystal vibrate, which produces an alternating potential difference across it.

cards.q: What is the difference between an A-scan and a B-scan?
cards.a: An A-scan shows the echoes as peaks on a graph against time, giving depths and distances along one line. A B-scan shows the echoes as dots whose brightness depends on their strength, building up a two-dimensional image.

cards.q: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of ultrasound imaging.
cards.a: Advantages: it uses no ionising radiation, and it gives moving images in real time with cheap, portable equipment. Disadvantages: its resolution is poorer than X-ray or MR imaging, and it cannot pass through bone or air-filled spaces such as the lungs.

cards.q: What is the difference between a coherent and a non-coherent bundle of optical fibres, and what is each used for in an endoscope?
cards.a: In a coherent bundle the fibres keep the same relative positions at both ends, so it carries an image back. In a non-coherent bundle they do not; it is cheaper and carries light in to illuminate.

cards.q: Give one use of an endoscope and one advantage of using it.
cards.a: Use: viewing inside the body, for example the stomach or a joint, or guiding keyhole surgery. Advantage: no large incision is needed, so recovery is quicker and the risk of infection is lower.

cards.q: Outline the basic principles of a magnetic resonance (MR) scanner.
cards.a: Hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field are excited by radio pulses and emit radio signals as they de-excite.
marks: The patient lies in the strong magnetic field of a superconducting magnet; hydrogen nuclei (protons) line up and precess about the field lines.
Gradient field coils vary the field across the body, so each small region can be picked out.
Short radio-frequency pulses excite the protons, changing their spin state.
As the protons de-excite they emit radio-frequency signals.
The signals are detected and processed by a computer to build an image of a cross-section.

cards.q: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of MR scanning.
cards.a: Advantages: no ionising radiation, and very good contrast between different soft tissues. Disadvantages: it is expensive and slow, and it cannot be used on patients with pacemakers or some metal implants.

cards.q: How are X-rays produced in an X-ray tube?
cards.a: Electrons from a heated filament are accelerated through a large potential difference and strike a metal target (the anode). About 1% of their kinetic energy becomes X-ray photons; the rest heats the target.

cards.q: An X-ray tube operates at 80 kV. Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays produced. λmin=1.6×10−11 m\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{min}} = 1.6 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{m}λmin​=1.6×10−11 m

cards.q: An X-ray spectrum has a continuous part and sharp characteristic lines. Explain how each is produced.
cards.a: The continuous part comes from electrons slowing down; the lines come from electron transitions in the target atoms.
marks: Continuous spectrum: electrons are decelerated by the target atoms and give up varying amounts of kinetic energy as photons, up to a maximum of eV\displaystyle eVeV.
Characteristic lines: an incoming electron knocks an electron out of an inner shell of a target atom.
An electron from a higher shell drops into the gap, emitting a photon whose energy equals the difference between the two levels.
These energies are fixed for the target element, so the lines are characteristic of it.

cards.q: In an X-ray tube, what controls the intensity of the beam, and what controls the maximum photon energy?
cards.a: The tube current (set by the filament current) controls the intensity: more electrons per second. The tube potential difference controls the maximum photon energy.
cards.why: The anode rotates so that the heat is spread over a larger area and the target does not melt.

cards.q: State two ways of reducing the dose a patient receives during an X-ray, and one way of making the image sharper.
cards.a: Dose: filter out low-energy X-rays with an aluminium filter (they would only be absorbed by the body), and use a sensitive detector so the exposure can be short. Sharpness: use a small source area on the anode and keep the patient still.

cards.q: Why is a patient given a barium meal before some X-ray images are taken?
cards.a: Soft tissues such as the gut absorb X-rays weakly, so they show little contrast. Barium has a high atomic number and absorbs X-rays strongly, so the organs it fills show up clearly.

cards.q: How does a flat panel detector form an X-ray image, and what are its advantages over photographic film?
cards.a: A scintillator converts X-rays to light, which falls on an array of photodiode pixels that are read electronically. It is more sensitive, so the dose is lower, and the image is digital: available at once and easy to enhance, store and share.

cards.q: Why is an intensifying screen used with photographic X-ray film?
cards.a: The screen absorbs X-rays and emits many visible photons, which expose the film much more efficiently. The exposure can be shorter, so the patient's dose is reduced.
cards.why: A fluoroscopic image intensifier does the same job for moving, real-time images.

cards.q: Write the equation for the attenuation of X-rays passing through a thickness x\displaystyle xx of material.
cards.a: I=I0e−μx\displaystyle I = I_{0}e^{-\mu x}I=I0​e−μx, where μ\displaystyle \muμ is the linear attenuation coefficient.

cards.q: Define half-value thickness, and state how it relates to the linear attenuation coefficient.
cards.a: The thickness of material that reduces the intensity of the beam to half. x12=ln⁡2μ\displaystyle x_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\mu}x21​​=μln2​.

cards.q: A material has a linear attenuation coefficient of 50 m−1\displaystyle 50\ \text{m}^{-1}50 m−1 for a beam of X-rays. Calculate its half-value thickness.
cards.a: 0.014 m
steps: x12=ln⁡2μ=0.69350\displaystyle x_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\mu} = \frac{0.693}{50}x21​​=μln2​=500.693​
x12=0.014 m\displaystyle x_{\frac{1}{2}} = 0.014\ \text{m}x21​​=0.014 m

cards.q: Define the mass attenuation coefficient.
cards.a: The linear attenuation coefficient divided by the density of the material: μm=μρ\displaystyle \mu_{m} = \frac{\mu}{\rho}μm​=ρμ​.

cards.q: Outline the basic principles of a CT scanner.
cards.a: A narrow X-ray beam is rotated round the patient and a computer builds cross-sections from the detector readings.
marks: An X-ray tube produces a narrow, monochromatic beam.
The tube moves in a circle round the patient.
An array of detectors on the opposite side records the intensity transmitted from each direction.
A computer processes the signals to produce an image of a slice through the body, and many slices give a three-dimensional picture.

cards.q: Give one advantage and two disadvantages of a CT scan compared with a simple X-ray image.
cards.a: Advantage: it gives detailed cross-sections and can distinguish tissues of similar density, with good resolution. Disadvantages: the patient receives a much higher dose of ionising radiation, and the equipment is expensive.

cards.q: State the properties that make technetium-99m a good medical tracer.
cards.a: It emits gamma radiation only, of an energy that suits gamma cameras (about 140 keV). Its half-life is about 6 hours: long enough for the scan, short enough to limit the dose. It can be attached to compounds that are taken up by particular organs.

cards.q: What is a molybdenum–technetium generator, and why is it important?
cards.a: It contains molybdenum-99, which has a half-life of about 66 hours and decays into technetium-99m. The technetium is washed out when needed. It lets a hospital have a supply of a short-lived tracer that could not survive being transported.

cards.q: Explain how a PET scan locates a tracer in the body.
cards.a: The tracer emits positrons, and each annihilation gives two gamma photons in opposite directions.
marks: The patient is given a tracer that emits positrons.
Each positron travels a very short distance and annihilates with an electron.
Two gamma photons are produced, travelling in opposite directions.
A ring of detectors records pairs of photons arriving at the same moment; the annihilation lies on the line between the two detectors, and a computer builds an image from many such lines.

cards.q: Define physical, biological and effective half-life, and state how they are related.
cards.a: Physical: the time for half the nuclei to decay. Biological: the time for the body to remove half the substance by natural processes. Effective: the time for the activity in the body to halve, from both together. 1TE=1TB+1TP\displaystyle \frac{1}{T_{E}} = \frac{1}{T_{B}} + \frac{1}{T_{P}}TE​1​=TB​1​+TP​1​.

cards.a: 4.0 hours
cards.why: The effective half-life is always shorter than either of the other two.

1TE=312=0.25 h−1\displaystyle \frac{1}{T_{E}} = \frac{3}{12} = 0.25\ \text{h}^{-1}TE​1​=123​=0.25 h−1
TE=4.0 hours\displaystyle T_{E} = 4.0\ \text{hours}TE​=4.0 hours

cards.q: Describe the structure and operation of a gamma camera.
cards.a: A collimator, a scintillator crystal, photomultiplier tubes and a computer.
marks: A lead collimator with many narrow parallel holes lets through only gamma photons travelling along the axis of the holes.
The photons strike a scintillator crystal, each producing a flash of light.
An array of photomultiplier tubes behind the crystal turns each flash into an electrical pulse.
A computer uses the pulses to work out where each photon arrived and builds an image of where the tracer is.

cards.q: How does a photomultiplier tube turn a faint flash of light into a measurable electrical pulse?
cards.a: A photon releases an electron from the photocathode. The electron is accelerated to a series of electrodes (dynodes), and at each one it knocks out several more electrons. The number multiplies at every stage, giving a large pulse.

cards.q: In external radiotherapy with high-energy X-rays, how is the dose to healthy cells limited?
cards.a: The beam is aimed at the tumour from several directions, or rotated round the patient, so the tumour gets the full dose while healthy tissue in any one path gets only a fraction. The beam is also shaped to the tumour and other areas are shielded.

cards.q: Why are beta emitters used for radioactive implants placed in or beside a tumour?
cards.a: Beta particles have a short range in tissue, so their energy is absorbed in the tumour and nearby healthy tissue receives very little.

cards.q: Compare X-ray imaging, MR scanning and ultrasound in terms of safety and image resolution.
cards.a: X-ray and CT: good resolution, but ionising radiation. MR: very good resolution and soft-tissue contrast, with no ionising radiation. Ultrasound: the safest and most convenient, but the poorest resolution.
